How long had it been since she felt the breeze upon her face? The gritty sensation of sand
underneath her? The scent of the sea wafting by? Even the night sky, brimming with stars as
the moon shone overhead, felt so infinitely vast and distant now – a sight she thought she had
long since gotten used to with her work. Yet now…
The words for her magecraft froze into a lump in her throat, paralyzed by the simple yet
overwhelming sensations. It made her feel… alive. So, so alive.
Then the breeze tugged at the hem of her blue coat, dousing her with the cold, stark reality.
No, she wasn’t. She died. The her of now was nothing more than a remnant – no, barely even
that. She was just a memory, a shred of thought shed by her original dying self that had been
rayshifted into the first singularity.
It was only thanks to Ren’s quick thinking and the Velvet Room’s power that she was saved,
yet she was inexorably linked to the latter. Her existence was unstable, rendering her unable
to exit unless she wanted oblivion.
In a sense, it was far more of a prison for her than it had been for Ren during his
‘rehabilitation’.
Sensations like this, things she had long since taken for granted, were lost to her - possibly
forever. The world was gone. Humanity was gone.
There was nothing left.
Olga felt eyes on her – and saw Ren staring at her, his expression unreadable. Instead of
speaking, he simply patted on the rock beside him. She blinked in surprise – and felt warmth
streaming down her cheeks.
She hurriedly wiped it away. When had she started crying?
Instead of explaining herself or speaking, she simply sat down next to him. Neither of them
said anything as stared up at the skies, the myriad stars dotting the infinite cosmos, as only
the sound of the waves filled the air.

Holding her knees close to herself, she closed her eyes tight as more tears squeezed out. So
many emotions, so much pain she had tried to shove away with her duty – to her family, to
Chaldea, to Ren, to everyone remaining. They all came at once. The tears wouldn’t stop. She
couldn’t stop them.
But not as a flood, just a gentle, constant stream. A slow releasing of painful pressure as she
took deep breaths.
In.
And out.
The former director chanced a glance at Ren. He was staring up at the stars, his expression
impassive yet patient. The attendant’s mouth dropped open slightly, wanting to speak to him.
But she soon closed it, and followed his gaze.
What could she say? What should she say?
Her entire life had been nothing but constant rug pulls from under her – losing her position as
heir to her valued colleague, becoming the director of Chaldea solely because her father
passed away at the worst timing possible, then betrayed by a demon god pillar masquerading
as her beloved mentor before almost being tossed into the burning inferno that was
CHALDEAS.
The only reason why she was even here right now was sitting beside her – who she slapped in
the face because he had fallen asleep at the commencement ceremony from jet lag. Even
then, she was denied the world, her world, simply because the Velvet Room didn’t have the
capabilities at the moment to properly restore her.
She could feel mad laughter clawing at her throat over how ridiculous it all was. It truly felt
like a comedic play – and she was its greatest jester.
But… just like her companion beside her, she didn’t have time for madness. Or exhaustion,
or pain or anything else. Humanity depended on their success.
They only had each other, and every moment she was manifested burdened Ren more to
maintain. Though he would never show it, this was yet another burden he took on. For their
mission. For humanity.
For her.
“I’m going to get started,” she whispered, her voice cracking slightly.
“Gotcha,” Ren quietly acknowledged. “I’ll be here if you need me.”
“I know.”
After a moment, she shakily stood back up. There would be time to cry more later. Right
now, she had a task to accomplish. Taking a deep breath, grasping what minutiae of
composure she had left, she stretched out her hand and summoned her personal astrolabe.

It was a far smaller model compared to the one in the Velvet Room, designed for portable
use. The mystic code floated above her hand and spun like a globe before darkening within,
turning into a replica of the night sky, complete with the stars and constellations as symbols
of the sun and moon rotated on the frames outside.
The magic crest on her forehead began to glow as she accessed her circuits. “Stars. Cosmos.
Gods. Animus. Antrum. Unbirth. Anima. Animusphere,” she chanted.
The frames around the astrolabe spun faster as the stars within slowly moved and shifted, the
constellations fading in and out of sight. Ren sat back to take in the sight. He hadn’t seen
Olga properly use her magecraft before, only the results. This was fascinating to witness.
She pointed down at the star mat. Both it and the telescope floated into the air, the former
sliding underneath the spinning astrolabe as the telescope faced the heavens, peering into the
sky. The sigils drawn by Ren began glowing brightly as the constellation designs on the mat
began shifting and moving as well.
Every tool of the ritual served a purpose. The astrolabe was her primary tool and focal point
of her magecraft. The sigils acted as a connection between her and Ren, allowing her to
utilize his magic circuits to process information. The telescope interfaced with said circuits to
update the star mat and astrolabe to the current era. The mat solidified the connection and
strengthened the purpose of the ritual.
All of them together brought about the realization of Olga Marie Animusphere, and allowed
her to interact with the world as she saw fit.
Glancing up at the night sky, she murmured an aria as she adjusted the astrolabe. Lifting it
higher, the frames started to slow down as the night sky within began settling. Constellations
winked in and out of focus as though it was searching a certain configuration.
Finally, it stilled, rotating gently as certain constellations and stars remained glimmering.
Olga looked up at the star-filled sky again and the Phantom Thief followed her gaze. Perhaps
it was his imagination, but were the stars that made the constellations glowing slightly
brighter than the others?
The attendant summoned her clipboard, wrote furiously on the clipboard while murmuring
calculations for herself, then ripped off the bottom part of the paper.
“Here,” she stated, handing it over to Ren. “These are coordinates to the most mystery dense
location I can currently detect. Tell Drake to head for this bearing and distance, she’ll
understand it.”
She gave a small sigh, but steadied herself. “With any luck, whatever you unearth will be
enough to satisfy both her greed and the Velvet Room’s request. And possibly even the
location of the grail, though I wouldn’t be too hopeful about that.”
He nodded as he took the paper. Taking a cursory look at the paper, all he saw was a string of
numbers and symbols that made no sense to him. Well, if Olga said Drake would understand

it, then he had no reason to doubt her. “Thanks as always,” he replied with a warm smile.
“You always come through for us.”
Olga frowned. “Don’t flatter me, Amamiya,” she muttered. “This is my duty – as it always
has been.” As it always should be. This whole mess had been her responsibility, and she had
failed time and time again no matter what she did. This wasn’t anywhere near enough to
make up for it. “Now if you’ll excuse me…”
“You don’t have to go back so soon, do you?” Ren asked. “I think I can keep you out for a
few minutes more at least.”
He smiled playfully at her. “I could use some company for star watching, you know?”
The attendant froze, words of admonition on the tip of her tongue. Yet once more, his words
had snagged upon that desire of hers, as it always did.
Finally, she sighed. “Very well,” she relented. “Bonding is necessary to your development,
after all.”
The Phantom Thief smiled happily. “Thanks, Olga.”
“Nothing to thank me about,” she brushed off again resignedly. Looking around, she picked
up the star map that had been the catalyst of the ritual earlier and handed the telescope back
to Ren. That done, she rolled it up into an impromptu pillow and set it on the rock before
laying down, resting her head on one side. The Master moved and laid down right next to her
in turn.
The width of the star map was barely wide enough for the two of them, but Olga didn’t mind.
At this point, they had watched the stars enough times together that she was used to it.
It was silent save for the lapping of the waves beneath them. They stared up at the stars
glimmering high above in the cloudless night. Infinitely distant and cold, yet holding their
own beauty that long since mesmerized humanity for eons. The rock underneath their backs
was hard and unyielding, yet its solidness held its own odd form of comfort.
“… What are you gonna do after all this?”
Olga blinked at the sudden question and looked over at Ren, mere inches away from her.
“Excuse me?” she asked.
“When we get the world back,” the Phantom Thief clarified. “You probably have a lot you
wanna do, right?”
The attendant’s mouth dropped open at the inanity of the statement, then she scoffed as she
glared back up at the sky.
“It isn’t that there’s much I want to do, so much as there’s so much that needs to be done,”
she sniffed. “First, I have to deal with all the official reports. So many rules and policies have
been broken out of necessity in order to fulfill the Grand Order, meaning the documents must
be doctored as much as possible to minimize liability.”

“And of course, there’s your, Morgana, and Ritsuka’s involvement as well. Three untrained
Masters, one of them smuggled in and is an animal, combined with your abilities, will invite
all sorts of questions and attention. Romani had already been editing the documents as we go,
but his work is… sloppy, despite his best efforts. The absurd quantity of paperwork I’ll have
to go through-“
Ren simply smiled as Olga rambled and ranted hotly about the sheer amount of work she had
to do once the dust had all settled. It confirmed to him that Olga’s place wasn’t the Velvet
Room – at least, not permanently. The real world was her home, and he would do everything
he could to bring it back for her. For all of them.
Yet, the sheer scope of her future bureaucratic suffering had him look over in playful concern.
“Do you need any help with that?” he asked earnestly. “My English probably needs some
more work, but I should be able to get up to speed to help with the less complicated jobs.”
The attendant sighed tiredly. “I appreciate the offer, but that is not necessary,” she waved off.
“You are already fighting to restore the world, a task that you are doing more than admirably
in. No, Amamiya, this is my battle. I have the powers, knowledge, and connections necessary
to see it all through, no matter how strenuous it is.”
She looked over at him, her citrine eyes hard and sharp as they met Ren’s steel-grey ones. “I
won’t fail my own duties, not again,” she pledged. “That I swear to you.”
The Phantom Thief smiled, reassured. “I know you won’t,” he acknowledged. “But again,
thank you, Olga. For before, now, and in the future.”
Olga narrowed her eyes slightly, then huffed again as she turned to look back up at the stars.
“You thank me too much,” she grumbled. Despite the darkness of the night, her pale skin was
illuminated by the moonlight, showing Ren the small blush on her cheeks. He couldn’t help
but chuckle slightly, causing her to blush deeper.
“What about you?” she immediately whirled on him. “What do you plan to do once the world
is restored and your contract is finished?”
“Me?” Ren mused. “Well, head back to Tokyo for one. With the payment from Chaldea, I
should be able to find a decent apartment there despite the ridiculously high rent. I’ll also
have to start studying again to get into university. Hopefully I won’t be too rusty after this
‘summer vacation’.”
“Under Lavenza’s, Lord El-Melloi’s, and my tutelage? I’d personally smack you upside the
head if you failed on that front,” the attendant remarked drily.
The Phantom Thief laughed. “Ha! Yeah, can’t argue there,” he acquiesced. “I also promised
my friends I’d treat them too. There was this one fancy hotel restaurant we went to one time
when it was just Morgana, Ann, and Ryuji. We went there after Kamoshida’s change of heart
to celebrate. That was where the Phantom Thieves were first formed.”
“A hotel restaurant?” Olga echoed in slight bafflement. “Were there no other establishments
you could visit?”

“Well, we only got thirty thousand yen from selling his gold medal,” he admitted ruefully.
“So we couldn’t exactly splurge at the fanciest places. But it was an all-you-can-eat buffet, so
we still got our money’s worth anyway. It was probably the best deal Iwai could give me, at
any rate.”
“A former yakuza, managing a model gun shop, acting as your fence,” the attendant
hummed. “Not unusual for a magus, admittedly, but for a civilian your connections are…
rather strange.”
“What can I say, I attract out of the ordinary types,” Ren chuckled. “We did manage to sell a
golden briefcase for a lot more money though and went out for sushi with it. Morgana missed
out on it though – we couldn’t take cats in, and the leftovers were sacrificed to Sojiro so we
could check his place.”
Slowly, his smile turned wistful as he pondered. “I wondered what they would’ve thought of
the fatty tuna we caught today,” he murmured. “They’d probably love it.”
“… You think they would join you?” Olga asked quietly.
“You wouldn’t have been able to stop them,” Ren replied with a small laugh. “Even if they
weren’t Masters, they would’ve done everything they could to join in. And if they couldn’t
join singularities, they would’ve been in the command center or doing everything they can.”
“Your companions sound like they would’ve been great assets for Chaldea,” the attendant
remarked.
“They would’ve accepted nothing less,” the Phantom Thief agreed. “If there’s one thing
common about all of them is that they can all be as stubborn as me at times.”
“I am now rescinding my earlier statement.”
They both laughed at the joke, their mirth resounding through the still air – then Ren shifted
and hissed as his circuits scalded his flesh.
Olga didn’t miss the sound, a quick glance confirming his condition. “I’ve overstayed,” she
stated bluntly, standing up and brushing sand off her dress. “I’ve put far too much of a burden
on you for my own selfishness-“
“Don’t,” Ren cut her off as he sat up as well, wincing slightly. “I was the one who asked you
to stay. It’s my fault this time, but I don’t regret any of it.”
He grinned. “If there’s another chance to bring you back out, I’ll take it,” he finished.
“That is an unacceptable risk, Amamiya,” she admonished him, frowning. “Your
consideration is deeply appreciated, but I can be patient enough to wait until the world has
been restored. Until then, our efforts should be solely focused on the mission so we may see
it to completion sooner. Am I understood?”
“… Yep, I do,” Ren replied, holding his hands up in surrender. “I won’t bring you out if it can
be helped.”

“Which means you will try to find some other method to,” she noted, annoyed. Finally, she
sighed. “Still… thank you, Ren, for allowing me a bit more time to enjoy the outside world
once more. I… I hadn’t realized I missed this.”
The Phantom Thief smiled gently. “Nothing to thank me for,” he brushed off. “I’ll see us all
home. I promise you.”
Olga paused, then nodded, smiling back in turn. Then her glow dimmed as her figure faded
away, as ephemeral as a ghost. A few seconds later, Ren stood by himself on the rock as the
lapping of waves filled the now quiet night air once more.
He didn’t immediately move, simply sighing as he felt his circuits finally cool down. Staring
up into the infinite cosmos now felt infinitely lonelier without Olga’s presence.
Finally, he struggled up with a grunt. Picking up the star mat, he folded it again and tucked it
away in his pocket before slowly, laboriously making his way down the rock. As he did, his
mind couldn’t help but wander to his friends. How would they have handled the singularities?
What would they have made of the Servants? There was so much he wanted to ask them.
Landing on the sand, he slowly turned to head back – then noticed some small, smooth rocks
laying on the foot of the outcrop. Picking one up, he bounced it in his hand and felt its solid
weight in his palm. Rearing his arm back, he threw it out over the ocean. It vanished in an
instant into the night over the black sea. He tried to pick out where it landed, but in vain.
A peal of distant laughter from the raucous party echoed through the air. For a moment, he
was in LeBlanc again. Ryuji and Morgana were busy arguing over the last potato chip,
unaware of Ann casually reaching over to grab it. Yusuke and Makoto were chatting about
the Sayuri, bringing up a few other works of art in their discussion.
Off to the side, he could see Haru and Sumire discussing the nutritional value of the former’s
vegetables and how they could be incorporated into a sports diet. Futaba was by them,
digging up recipes and the average numbers on said vegetables, unaware they’d drag her into
trying other foods besides curry and yakisoba.
Beside him, he could hear the gurgling of the percolator going off. Reflexively, he turned to
grab a cupAnd suddenly, he was back on the beach. The chatter of his friends was replaced by the
gentle lapping of the sea, the slightly chilly night breeze instead of the warmth of the café. In
his hand was simply another rock – smooth, round, and solid like the others.
He shook his head. Any cups would be infinitely far away now, back in Japan… and
probably consumed by fire.
“Master? Is everything alright?”
The sound of Martha’s voice caused him to jump slightly in surprise. “Oh, yeah, I’m fine,” he
quickly reassured her with a grin. “Just wanted to step away for a bit. It’s a nice night, after
all.”

“It certainly is,” the saint agreed. As Ren turned back to throwing another rock, she simply
stared at him.
Truth was, she had got here a bit before, just as her Master had descended from the rock. She
wondered what she would witness when he was by himself. When he didn’t have to wear a
mask for anyone, so to speak. Her doubts, despite David’s counsel, still gnawed away in her
heart and mind.
What she saw was unexpected in how… mundane it was. Instead of a devil or an angel, she
simply saw a very tired young man, lost in his thoughts. Nothing either good or evil, just
simply someone who had much on his mind.
It reminded her of a stark fact: They had all been summoned to help save and preserve the
world, and they answered, her included. And while there were three Masters, it was Ren who
was bearing the lion’s share of the burden.
Despite that, he dissuaded everyone’s fears and anxieties with a grin. He treated his peers, the
Servants, and the staff well, and was indeed a kind, compassionate man. At this point, that
was beyond doubt.
Yet the image of his exhaustion and profound melancholy only begged a question: What of
his fears and anxieties? Who helps assuage them in turn?
Thinking about it, she didn’t really know him. He readily shared details about himself with
no fuss, but that wasn’t the same.
Amidst the crowd, Ren perfectly melded with them – and perhaps for that same reason was
why he stood out so much.
“It’s hard to get a moment’s peace with Drake’s crew,” Martha commented, walking up
beside him. “I can understand why you’d like some quiet.”
“Right?” Ren chuckled as he stretched – and tried to hide a wince from Martha as his sore
muscles pulled. “I’m starting to see why Morgana complained so much about sailing with the
Romans back in the last singularity – it’s fun, but it’s crowded. Not much privacy for
anything.”
“And we unfortunately aren’t like Medea, who can simply create a bounded field for her
privacy,” the Rider sighed dejectedly.
“Think she’d make one for us if we asked?” the Phantom Thief mused.
“You’d be trying her patience.”
“True – she definitely doesn’t have the patience of a saint.”
“No, she does- wait, what is that supposed to mean?”
The Master burst out laughing at Martha’s indignant reply and reached for another rock. The
saint huffed, then blinked.

Once again, she had gotten caught up in his pace as everyone always did. She needed to find
a way to help him with his melancholy, but, how would she be able to…?
She watched as Ren proceeded to throw another rock toward the ocean. Suddenly, a flash of
inspiration struck her mind. Eagerly, she asked Tarrasque for a favor and relayed the plan to
her. The dragon groaned in displeasure like a child told to do something unpleasant.
‘You treat me too rough, sis,’ he complained. ‘Fine. Do what ya gotta. At least I’m not getting
pummeled half to death this time…’
Martha stepped up with a wry smile. “Master, would you mind giving this rock a toss?” she
asked.
Ren looked over in surprise as he accepted the rather large rock. It was circular and flat,
reminding him of a discus he had seen during the Olympic games, albeit rounder. It was hard
to see the details in the moonlight, but he could pick out a spiked top and six different holes
on the sides…
His eyes widened in realization as he realized what he was holding. “No way,” he gasped.
“Is… Is this Tarrasque?”
In reply, the lion-like head popped out of the central hole and let out a low growl – though it
sounded more akin to a cub’s meow than its normal roar.
“Hahaha, he’s so tiny, and so cute! Can he just do that!?”
“I asked him for a small favor,” Martha explained with a grin. “While I have… tested his
endurance no small number of times, I’ve always been curious about his ability to fly.
Dragons are said to be masters of the sky, aren’t they?”
Tarrasque huffed at the saint for the comment but otherwise made no other sound.
“Now, let’s see how far you can fling him, Master,” the Rider requested, smiling as Ren
continued to make rather cute sounds holding the tiny dragon. “Don’t worry, I’m sure he’ll be
fine.”
It was simply the first idea that came to mind, and a very haphazard one. But when her
master was so resistant to her normal methods of aid, she had to get…creative.
Even Tarasque ultimately agreed with that, so this should be a safe outlet.
Probably.
A grin, happier and larger than she had seen in a while, spread across the Phantom Thief’s
face. It was a level of, almost concerningly honest enthusiasm she’d never seen from him.
The saint smiled, relieved at how his mood already seemed to be lifting… and faded as his
circuits began glowing. “Masks of my rage, become my wings of rebellion,” he intoned.

His right arm suddenly began growing and swelling, the skin turning green as it extended
well beyond what was humanly possible. Tarrasque was still clenched in his hand, though
now he looked more like a pebble in the gigantic arm’s grip.
“With a once in a lifetime chance like this, you gotta do this right!”
Oh boy.
‘Sis?’ Tarrasque called out worriedly.
Martha could only give an apologetic smile as she stepped backward to his fate. ‘I’ll call you
back if you get flung too far,’ she reassured him. ‘But don’t worry. I’m sure Ren won’t harm
you. I think.’
The dragon was about to speak when suddenly, he was spun. With a mighty twist and a
hearty roar, he was flung straight over the ocean!
‘Sis, whyyyyy…..?!?’
“Is that… ninety meters? Nice!”
She looked over at Ren as the young man’s eyes had turned red to see where Tarrasque had
landed. He was laughing uproariously all the while as his arm slowly returned to its normal
shape, and he turned to her.
“Hey, your eyes are better than mine. Ninety, you think?”
The saint could only smile to herself. Truly, Ren was simply a young man… and her Master.
“Yes, around ninety meters is accurate. You can trust your own eyes.”
“Let’s go!” He shouted with a playful pump of his arm, and she giggled.
She wouldn’t waver any longer. She wasn’t in the service of a devil or an angel. Just someone
who had their own burdens and methods, tempered by kindness and compassion if not
wisdom. It would be an honor to fight alongside them.
“Hey, do you think you can call Tarrasque back?” Ren asked, his eyes glimmering eagerly
even in the dark of the night. “I think I can get him even farther!”
Martha’s smile turned into one of exasperation. While he wasn’t a demon, he certainly could
be an imp.
Their trials were only beginning.

Chapter 123: Dive

If something is worth doing, then it won't be easy.

Chapter Notes

“So I simply need to wipe it down and oil it?”
The holographic image of Artoria, projecting from the communicator, nodded.
“Indeed,” the king of knights confirmed. “While weapons for the most part require regular
maintenance, the work necessary isn’t too strenuous. Sharpening may be occasionally done
as well, but I do not think it is needed here.”
Mash nodded thoughtfully as she leaned over from her hammock she was sitting on and
picked up an oily rag – something the Golden Hind had in spades. Laying on her lap was her
sword, still glimmering beautifully from the faint sunlight streaming from the distant hatches.
Lifting it up, she looked over the blade closely. Despite its harrowing debut, there wasn’t a
single scratch or nick marring its beauty. The edge was still as sharp as when she first beheld
it without the slightest chip or dent. It remained as perfect as the day she received it.
She looked back at the gross, oily rag she held in her hand. Suddenly, she felt much less
certain about applying it to her blade.
“I understand your hesitation.” The Shielder looked over at Artoria, who was smiling
patiently and with a hint of amusement.
“Well made conceptual weapons don’t lose their edge or sheen unless by exceptional
circumstances,” the king stated. “Noble phantasms even less so. While most pages are
quickly made to become accustomed to oiling blades, it must feel rather unnecessary here for
a multitude of reasons.”

Mash hesitated then hung her head guiltily. “It’s a precious gift from senpai, and a beautiful
weapon besides,” she admitted. “It just feels like I’m dirtying it for no good reason.”
Then suddenly, a thought came to her mind. “Did you maintain your swords similarly,
Artoria?” she asked, tilting her head in curiosity.
The Saber nodded in confirmation. “It was more of a habit than anything, but yes,” she
answered. “Mythical weapon or no, I would not risk it failing me by overlooking something
so fundamental. Neglecting maintenance and taking its strength for granted is to disrespect
both the weapon and to the craftsmen who had made them.”
“Disrespecting both the weapon and the craftsmen…” the Shielder murmured. She took a
deep breath, gulped her down hesitance, then began wiping down the blade with the rag.
“Beware of your hand as you clean and oil your sword,” Artoria warned, observing her
careful movements. “More than once I’ve seen a page or squire slice their hand with a
careless wipe.”
“Understood,” Mash acknowledged as she cautiously worked on the blade. Despite the grime
on the rag, the blade didn’t stain. If anything, it seemed to take on a slight iridescent shine
from the oil applied.
“I hadn’t realized that maintenance would be so… simple,” she commented as she continued
her work. “I thought rusting would be a more prevalent problem in your time.”
“It is for the more negligent retainers,” the king acknowledged. “Aside from wiping away
water and blood, the oil prevents moisture from getting into the metal and causing rust to set
in. Armor was similarly treated, as well as painted or blued to help maintain its integrity.”
The Shielder frowned thoughtfully. She thought she had seen something like that during her
studies but nothing in detail. When she had the opportunity, a refresher on medieval arms and
armor might be in order.
“That said…” Artoria mused. “My knights sometimes could be rather careless. Tristan in
particular was guilty.”
Mash hadn’t expected to hear that particular fact. “Was he really?” she asked, surprised. “I
thought the knights of the Round Table were rather disciplined.”
“For the most part they were,” the Saber agreed. “But Tristan was often too absorbed in
either playing his harp or composing another song to the delight of his lover, Isolde. The
knights often had their squires take turns maintaining his gear.”
“Was it a common occurrence?” the Shielder asked as she continued to work on her word.
“Common enough that eventually Agravain took Tristan to task for it,” Artoria replied with a
small laugh. “He sat him down in a separate hall and proceeded to lambast and lecture him
for an entire morning and afternoon. By the time supper came around, he returned to us
ashen pale.”

“Agravain was truly that fierce?” Mash inquired, her eyes wide.
“His lectures certainly were,” the king responded with a fond smile. “Certainly no one
wished to incur his wrath. Thereafter, my subjects made sure to carry out his tasks with extra
diligence. Administration certainly became more efficient for about a week or so.”
“He sounds very helpful,” the girl commented. “If we end up summoning him, perhaps he
can assist the doctor with his paperwork.”
“More likely he’ll glare at Romani until he finally finishes,” Artoria drily corrected.
The Shielder made a mental note to check the scheduling of poor Romani’s shifts. Perhaps
she could convince Artemis or more likely Marie to relieve him more often…
“What prompted you to draw the sword?”
The sudden question abruptly dragged Mash out of her thoughts. Looking over in surprise,
she saw Artoria scrutinizing her closely.
“You would not have drawn the blade unless you felt it was necessary,” the latter pointed out.
“Indeed, your shield more than suffices as a weapon. While the serpent undoubtedly was a
formidable foe, I believe there is another reason you have done so.”
The Shielder’s mouth dropped slightly open, then she closed it. Staring into the blade, her
angular reflection stared back at her as she considered how to properly answer. She could feel
the calm, patient gaze of the king – curious and slightly pointed, but gentle and
nonjudgemental.
The answer felt simple… then why was it so hard to word it properly? Why was it difficult to
speak about? Now that she rolled the idea around in her head, it almost felt childish. As Joan
said, any goal was better than none, but in front of someone so grand, was it truly enough?
“… May I ask you a question first, Artoria?” Mash quietly inquired in turn.
“You may,” she allowed.

In a moment, it embraced her body, sinking deep into her magical flesh and sinew and almost

She opened one eye as rose petals floated by her in the bath. Although roses were her

The possibilities were endless. A bath that could delight everyone in its splendor was her

But that came later. Tomlin had done wonders for the bath already, and Nero wasn’t about to
pile yet more tasks on her so soon. No, this was quite ideal in its own way already.
For now, she simply sighed and closed her eyes as she relaxed. She could feel herself almost

“Hm, it seems I had missed out during my time in the Roman singularity. This is

Loki leaned in close. “I don’t care whether you love him or not,” they hissed. “But if you

The emperor could only heave heavy breaths as she clutched at her neck. The only sound that

For a moment, her vision flickered – and she was lying in the distant plains once more, far

She had lain there for three days and two nights. No one found her. No one cared to. For all
the love she had given her people, none of them loved her in turn. Her last sight was of the

Loki’s blood-red eyes and demonic glare flashed in her mind, scorching itself upon her soul.

Panicked, Nero flung the dagger away from her, as far as she could muster. It vanished into

Collapsing back into the bath, she heaved ragged breaths as she clutched at her arms, nails

No, no, Loki was gone. The dagger was gone. That time was gone. It was gone. All gone.
Shakily reaching up to the nearby bath implements, she took hold of a eucalyptus sprig. As

It was fine. This bath was the ideal method to relax. She was sure of it. It simply needed to be

As cold as that final sunsetNero’s grip tightened on the branch, causing the wood to begin creaking under her grip, as

Raising her arm, she began unsteadily brushing her limb with the eucalyptus. The scent of the

dull ache behind her eyes too.
The emperor shook her head as if to drive away the pain, but it was to no avail. She was
wearier than she thought.
Rest. She needed to rest.
Taking the sprig, she stroked downward on her arm in a final flourish – then gasped as a

skin, made by the dagger she held in herWith another broken cry, she dropped the eucalyptus sprig into the bath as though it had burst

She barely had time to cry out as she plunged into the water. It scalded her face and neck, the

But the worst of it was the throbbing in her head. It was far worse now, as though it was
being torn to shreds from within, and taking what remained of her mind with it.
Nero tried to breathe – and only felt scalding heat enter her nostrils and mouth, choking and

Was she about to die again? Again?! Ridding the world of her beauty and art once was

As blades dragged along the inside of her skull and brain, she could only whimper, the sound

Praetor, my praetor, please… save me…

The fog of pain and water ever so slightly lifted from the emperor’s vision, letting her see a

Her mind, her head, her affairs, her affections. It was all a mess. She couldn’t think straight,

But she… she was the Emperor of Roses. This was nothing. She had pushed through this

She needed to…
Dragging herself to a nearby pillar, she weakly reached up and grabbed a small ledge jutting

This… this situation would not stand. She wouldn’t allow it.
Slowly, a plan began forming at the furthest fringes of Nero’s tattered mind. Something to
help decisively resolve at least one situation here. It coalesced and solidified, coming into
view with greater clarity and weight until it dominated her thoughts.

It was simple: she would meet with Ren and they would have an outing together. When it
came to affection, what better way was there than to meet it head on? There she would find

her other self plaguing her mind.
The emperor almost laughed deliriously at her own genius. A brilliant plan. It… it simply
needed the details planned out, but the core was solid enough. Yes, that would be the greatest
method to resolve it all. This way, she would not betray anyone; not her Praetor, not Ren.
And especially not herself.
Taking a deep breath, feeling the steam filling her lungs, she slowly staggered toward the
changing room, dragging a towel with her while doing so. Her legs felt as unsteady as a
newborn fawn’s but she made her way regardless.
For today, at least, she had quite enough of baths.

“Be careful, Joker,” his best friend warned. “If you’re in trouble, just send some sort of signal
and I’ll head down there right away.”
“Bring us some souvenirs,” the redhead simply replied, matching his smile. It may have been
his imagination, but it seemed more strained and wearier than before.
Joan frowned at him but otherwise simply nodded, then marched off to the back of the ship to
keep watch.
With their farewells said, Ren hopped over the side of the ship. Grabbing the rope, he
rappelled down with ease on the side of the ship and landed solidly on Tarrasque’s back. The
footing was slightly inconvenient given the slopes of the spikes and the moisture of the sea,
but it was manageable.
Reaching down, he patted the dragon. “Hey Tarrasque,” he greeted. “No hard feelings about
the other night?” The legendary creature let out a loud snort, blasting a small wave of water
in front, but otherwise had no other reaction.
The Phantom Thief smiled ruefully. He would have to prepare something to apologize later.
There was a flash of golden light, and Siegfriend and Martha appeared beside him as Mash
soon joined him on the dragon’s back. “Are you ready, Master?” Siegfried asked.
“Ready as I’ll ever be,” the Phantom Thief answered. “Let’s go!”
The dragonslayer nodded. All four crouched down and grabbed hold of a spike. Ren grasped
his own - then frowned. It was far more slippery than he expected. He wouldn’t be able to get

a good grip. The others didn’t seem to be having problems in comparison, making up for it
with their supernatural strength.
“Hey Mash,” he called over. “Do you mind if I grab on to you instead? I can’t get a good
hold on Tarrasque’s spikes.”
The Shielder’s eyes widened in surprise as her face flushed. Unknown to her, Siegfried and
Martha were peering over in curiosity, the former with a small smile and the latter with a
raised eyebrow. “Er, o-of course, senpai,” she barely managed to stammer.
The Phantom Thief grinned. “Thanks so much, Mash,” he replied. Sidling over behind her, he
wrapped his arms around her waist, making sure to have a good grip. “Does this work?” he
checked.
Mash gulped as she squeezed Tarrasque’s spike harder. “Y-yes, that’s fine,” she answered,
keeping her eyes straight ahead. Right now, looking at her senpai was an impossible task.
“Pl-please hold on tight!”
Ren nodded. “You got it,” he acknowledged, then looked over to the other two and nodded in
affirmation.
“We’re diving,” Martha called out. “In three. Two. One!”
On the saint’s count, Tarrasque swam forward and then down. The surface of the ocean raced
up towards them like a subtle yet all-consuming wave, swiftly plunging them underwater. A
wall of foam and bubbles floated up, obscuring their vision at first but soon drifted away, like
a white curtain for a show being lifted.
And what Ren saw mystified him.
An endless blue space stretched before him on all sides. Sunlight filtered through the surface
of the sea, shattering them into sparkling rays that danced and glittered like countless
spotlights. The distance beyond was shrouded in azure, carrying with it the promise of
mystery, adventure – and danger.
As the dragon began dipping down, his view was pulled toward the depths. He couldn’t even
see the bottom, nor even darkness. All he could see was a deeper shade of blue stretching on
to infinity. In this expanse, there was nothing else besides himself, his Servants, the ship, and
Tarrasque. The smallness of his own existence was laid out before his eyes.
And yet despite it all, it was absolutely…
‘Beautiful.’
Mash’s thoughts whispered in his mind idly, like a comforting whisper. ‘Yeah, it is,’ he
quietly agreed.
No wonder why so many people fell in love with the sea, with all its harshness and dangers.
He wondered if this was what Drake felt each time she set out on her voyages.

‘Communications check.’
The curt voice of Medea cut across his sense of wonder as her words floated in through his
ear cuff. ‘Reading you loud and clear,’ Ren reported. ‘How are we looking so far?’
‘I do not detect any mysteries or hostiles within the vicinity,’ Medea replied. ‘However, the
concentration of magic is still relatively light near the surface. It will get thicker as you swim
into the depths.’
‘Roger that,’ the Phantom Thief acknowledged. ‘In that case, down we go.’ Looking over to
Martha, he gave a gesture to continue. The saint nodded in reply and a moment later,
Tarrasque began diving into the murky depths.
Clinging onto his sturdy Kouhai, he looked himself over. Despite being underwater, he was
breathing normally, with his vision unhindered by the water. While he still experienced the
weightlessness of being underwater and the water resistance brushing against him, he felt
almost completely dry.
Looking around him, it seemed like Mash, Siegfried, and Martha were in a similar state.
‘Enchantments are holding up so far,’ he noted, broadcasting his thoughts not only to Medea
but also to his companions. ‘How’s everyone else?’
‘Quite comfortable, all things considered,’ Siegfried noted.
‘No problems here, senpai,’ the Shielder responded. The water current had pushed her up
against him, but she hadn’t seemed to notice. The Phantom Thief decided to not mention it
for the time being.
‘Aside from the rather odd sensation of being underwater without the attendant dangers, I’m
doing fine as well,’ Martha answered.
‘Good to hear,’ the Caster responded. ‘Report to me if anything changes.’
Ren smiled as she cut off contact. His eyes turned red again as he activated his red eye to
scan their surroundings – and blinked as the fierce, bright blue glow of Tarrasque temporarily
blinded him. Nevertheless, it was a reassuring sight.
Looking up, he peered into the ocean around him. Within the murk, he saw glimmers of
different lights like stars in an evening sky – a few blue dots, many more yellow points… and
a small number of red ones. Most of them were at a distance, but he eyed them warily just in
case.
Suddenly, he felt a tug on his sleeve. ‘Senpai, over there,’ Mash gasped.
Deactivating his Third Eye, he turned to look – and his eyes widened as he saw a pod of sea
creatures swimming by. They were each the size of cars, with great fins both in front and
back as they smoothly glided through the water a distance away. He could barely make out
their eyes – beady black dots that hovered over their extended mouths.

They watched them as they swam by above them, seemingly unknowing or unconcerned with
their presence. ‘What are those, Medea?’ Ren asked.
There was a pause. ‘… I do not know,’ the witch admitted. ‘Most likely a type of phantasmal
species. Poseidon’s domain was far vaster than many mortals comprehend. His subjects were
spread far and wide, some of them never revealing themselves to humanity save via spare
glances.’
‘Makes sense,’ the Phantom Thief mused. ‘Even during modern times, the oceans are far less
explored than the land.’
He leaned over to look at Mash’s face. The wonder and awe in her eyes brought a warm smile
to his face. ‘What do you think of the sea?’ he asked.
The Shielder started a bit in surprise at the question, then turned toward him and beamed. ‘It
is wonderful, senpai,’ she breathed. ‘The surface was already breathtaking, but diving
underneath like this… it’s like I’m entering another world entirely. The recordings I have seen
pale in comparison.’
Then she noticed how close their faces were and immediately turned away, feeling heat
suffuse her face once more. They had been close like this a few times before, so why was she
now so self-conscious of it?
Meanwhile, Ren couldn’t help but laugh. ‘Yeah, the ocean documentaries I’ve seen really
undersell it,’ he agreed. ‘And they were pretty cool to watch. But then, we are in a mystical
ocean. Think that changes things?’
‘I believe the sea holds its own grandeur, no matter the age,’ Siegfried supplied, causing the
two to look over in curiosity. ‘Though the modern world likely has less phantasmal beings
within, it doesn’t change the power and beauty of the ocean.’
‘And storms are just as dangerous for those looking to traverse it,’ Martha added. ‘Sailors
have a dangerous duty no matter the era.’
‘Then maybe I should become a sailor,’ the Phantom Thief joked. ‘Adventure, danger, and
mystery all wrapped in one soaked package – what’s not to love?’
‘Master!’ the Rider groaned as Siegfried let out a hearty laugh and Mash giggled in response.
Through the ear cuff Ren could also sense Medea’s irritation through her frosty silence. He
could only chuckle at the outrage.
Further and further down Tarrasque dived. Darkness closed in on them, slowly but surely.
The glimmering rays of sunlight gradually faded into a glow above that steadily dimmed. It
was quiet all around them, with only the dragon’s feet stroking through the water reaching
their ears.
Then a low, hissing growl echoed through the depths, vibrating the very sea around them.

Tarrasque immediately stopped his dive, baring his fangs in preparation for a fight. In their
free hands, everyone summoned their weapons while still clinging on to the dragon’s back
spikes, bracing themselves for impact. Mash instinctively reached down with her free hand
and grasped Ren’s arm around her. Securing him as the Phantom Thief raised his pistol.
For a moment, nothing happened. They were still alone through the dark, shrouded depths.
Despite that, Ren could feel a presence close by, powerful and almost overbearing. He began
accessing his Third Eye again to check his surroundingsSuddenly, a gigantic sea serpent drifted above them. Dwarfing even Tarrasque, it was difficult
to make out any detail about it in the shadow save the size. They watched in silence as it
swam past, its great sinuous length gliding through the water like a river amidst the sea.
Another growl rumbled through the depths, causing the waters to quake once again. Despite
that, it never stopped or turned, instead simply swimming on. After what felt like an eternity,
they finally saw its tail, gently whipping and lashing through the water like a rudder, then that
too faded into the silent murk of the depths.
‘Medea, you there?’ Ren called out. Even his own mental voice was quiet, wishing not to
disturb the quiet of the darkened sea.
‘I hear you, though only just,’ the witch replied. ‘The concentration of magical energy is
getting stronger. I’m adjusting to compensate.’
‘You were not aware of such a large creature within our vicinity?’ Siegfried inquired.
‘Only once it drew near,’ the Caster admitted. ‘It is currently like scrying through fog. There
is only so much I can do remotely with little preparation. Again, I advise caution.’
‘It’s good we have Tarrasque with us,’ Martha murmured as the dragon continued swimming
down now that the threat had passed. ‘Otherwise, that might’ve gotten very bad.’
‘Senpai, are you alright?’ Mash quickly asked in concern, looking behind her.
Ren smiled. In response, he twisted his hand and gave hers a squeeze. ‘I am, thanks to you,’
he replied. ‘Thanks again for looking out for me, Mash.’
The Shielder was still clearly tense as she held her protective grip on his arm, but she still
managed a smile nevertheless. ‘Of course, Senpai,’ she murmured. ‘I won’t let anything hurt
you.’
‘And you’re doing a great job of that,’ he remarked – and glanced down in slight surprise
when she unconsciously pulled him closer.
He chuckled to himself. Mash could be surprisingly smooth when she wasn’t thinking about
it, he should try to instigate it a bit more often.
Deeper and deeper they dived. Cerulean waters gave way to azure, then inky blue. And it
only became yet darker as they continued their voyage. The sunlight above them was nothing

more than a fading spot of light, rapidly vanishing from view. Darkness descended – or rather
ascended – shrouding the murky seas and plunging them into the abyss.
The Phantom Thief looked around them. The figures of Tarrasque, his Servants, and Mash
were barely visible, as though they were outlined by a faint glow. Likely another
enchantment of Medea’s to ensure they could locate and see each other, just in case. He
wondered if their visibility was generally enhanced for the darkness, but there was nothing
else to see.
Before long, there was nothing. It felt as though everything in existence was removed. In the
depths of the ocean, even the very concept of light seemed utterly alien. Save for the feeling
of water brushing past them, it almost seemed as though they weren’t moving whatsoever.
Only the sound of Tarrasque’s great limbs told them otherwise.
Every so often, a sound echoed through the sea – a growl, a hiss, even at times a scream or
screech. They always were some great distance away, yet the adrenaline spiked through his
system each time. He checked each time with his Third Eye, yet he saw nothing. Whether it
was because they were too far or were concealed from him in some way, he couldn’t tell.
The gloom of the depths felt suffocating, and the water wasn’t helping. Was there nothing
there or were they being watched? He could feel goosebumps on his arms at the mere
thought.
After what felt like an eternity passed, a voice barely reached Ren’s mind. ‘You are nearing
the seafloor, Master,’ Medea reported. Her voice was barely audible, sounding incredibly
distant and muffled.
‘Got it,’ the Phantom Thief replied. ‘Thanks as always, Medea.’
Cutting off contact, he looked over at the others. They were still visible thanks to the witch’s
enchantments, but only just. ‘We’re almost to the bottom,’ he explained. ‘Can we stop here?
Don’t want Tarrasque disturbing the seabed and possibly burying the treasure.’
Martha nodded and glanced up toward Tarrasque’s head. A moment later, the dragon slowed
down then stopped, floating like an island amidst the abyss. ‘What are we going to do now,
Master?’ she inquired.
‘If I’m correct, the treasure should be just underneath us,’ he mused. ‘You guys stay up here
and keep watch, make sure no predators or some other thing sneaks up on us. I’ll head down,
locate it, then we’ll have Tarrasque haul it back up.’
‘S-senpai, that’s far too risky!’ Mash cried, turning back towards him. Though her face was
completely hidden in shadow, he could easily imagine her worried expression. ‘Please, at
least allow me to accompany you for your protection!’
Ren grinned. ‘Thanks Mash, but in this case, it’s probably safer if I go alone,’ he explained.
‘Here, let me show you.’

Releasing his grip around Mash’s waist, he gently kicked himself off Tarrasque’s back, to the
shock of the others. His circuits began glowing faintly as he once again reached for his
metaphorical mask.
‘Masks of my soul,’ he inwardly intoned as he ripped it off. ‘Become my wings of rebellion!’
In moments, seaweed-like tentacles and strands sprouted from his waist and legs. Growing at
a rapid pace, they soon extended past his legs before loosely bunching together at the end,
turning them into an approximation of a tail. Despite the dense tangle that now surrounded
them, his legs felt well unimpeded.
The Phantom Thief smirked. He knew Kelpie wouldn’t let him down.
‘Master?’ the saint called out in concern. ‘Are you alright?’
In response, Ren swam toward them. Despite the loose feeling of his ‘tail’, he glided through
the water as swiftly as any fish. Deciding to test its limits, he sped up and dove past them,
looping around Tarrasque at almost dizzying speeds.
It felt almost as exhilarating as his first flight. Almost.
Popping up in front of Tarrasque, he gave the great dragon’s surprised features a grin before
swimming back up. He relished the surprised expressions of Mash and his Servants as he
drifted down next to them. ‘I think that’ll do it,’ he concluded.
‘Another form?’ Siegfried commented, squinting through the dark to try and get a better
view. ‘You have taken to your new magecraft with gusto, it seems.’
‘Can’t argue there; I feel like a kid in a toy store,’ Ren admitted with a small laugh. ‘But
yeah, I’m a pretty fast swimmer like this – probably fast enough to make my way back to you
guys before something decides to take a bite out of me. Having too many of us go may alert
something, so it’s better if I search by myself.’
‘Are you certain about this?’ Martha worriedly asked. ‘Even Medea can’t detect what may
lurk on the bottom, and this short distance may still be too far for us to reach you in time.’
‘I won’t play around here,’ the Phantom Thief promised them. ‘I’m strictly looking for the
treasure then relaying the location to you guys. Once we get it, we’re out of here.’
‘Senpai…’ Mash began, then paused. He looked over in curiosity as she seemed to wrestle
with her words. ‘Please stay safe,’ she finally finished, almost pleading.
He smiled in reply. ‘I promise,’ he answered. Turning downward, he dove deeper into the
depths. In the darkness of the depths, even the great figure of the dragon soon faded into the
void.
Ren breathed a soft sigh as he swam toward the depths. Reaching up, he gently rubbed his
eyes through his eyelids, feeling a faint ache pulsing behind them. At least the dizziness from
the hangover had alleviated before setting out.

He wasn’t sure how much he had drunk, but he remembered growing sleepy and dozing off.
Apparently, after he had passed out, Siegfried had by Drake’s request surreptitiously carried
him back to his hammock to sleep it off.
A slight frown creased his lips as he kept swimming down through the darkness. Despite that,
he still remembered everything: every thought he had, the taste of the sack… and every word
he had said. He thought he had mastered holding his tongue, but he greatly underestimated
the power of alcohol.
It was frustrating, he had to admit, that for all his efforts he could still be peeled open so
easily. Secrets just spilled out with barely any prompting from the captain. His thoughts on
Chaldea, his worries, fears, goals and pains… such information could do a lot of damage if
the wrong ears heard.
Beyond even the sting from his own frailty, it was dangerous.
The Phantom Thief could only let out a quiet sigh, a sound that was almost terrifyingly loud
in the silent depths. For now, it seemed only Drake had heard him, and she wasn’t the type to
blather about his secrets.
Once more, he checked to make sure Mash’s protection against toxins and poisons was active
again. He honestly felt ridiculous for how paranoid he was getting about it, but getting drunk
once was far more than enough for him.
He would handle it just like he always had: Drawing strength from others until he could stand
and march forward, no matter the burden. That was his promise to himself, and what the
world needed.
Pushing aside his ruminations for now, he continued diving deeper. Compared to the surface,
the seawater now was frigid, chilling him down to the bone. He was sure Medea’s
enchantments were the only thing keeping him from a frigid death.
The darkness was just as disorienting as the cold. It was impossible to tell which way was up,
down, left, or right. The bubbles filtering upwards from his breath were the only sense of
direction he had.
His eyes turned red as he activated his Third Eye again. But even then it hardly made a
difference: though his own body and the sea floor came into view through grey outlines, the
sheer absence of the depths left nothing for his enhanced eyes to process at all.
Taking a breath to steady himself, he continued diving. This was far different than being in a
pitch-black room. On solid land, he had options. Whether it was inching his way across the
ground, finding a wall or an object and figuring out by touch, or simply sensing the shift in
the air around him, he could at least get some sense of his bearings.
But here, in the depths of the sea that had possibly never seen light before, there was no such
luck. Not only did the darkness rob him of sight, the water also muffled his hearing, smell,
and sense of touch. He could’ve swum straight into a cave or a mouth of a sea monster and he
wouldn’t have been able to tell.

Despite the openness of the ocean and Medea’s enchantments, it felt suffocating. It felt like
he was in a prison almost tailor-made for him.
A pang of fear surged through his body and clutched at his heart – a familiar sensation for
him and one he accepted. Only an idiot wouldn’t be at least somewhat afraid here. But he
would manage, as he always did. Fear was an old companion of his at this point, after all.
‘Still there, Medea?’ he called out.
‘… -rely,’ came the witch’s voice, distorted and faint. ‘… interference… ard to…. municate….
still… racking…’
‘I can barely hear you, Medea,’ he replied. ‘Just shout if anything hostile’s coming my way.’
There was no answer, nor did he expect one. Probably from the sheer density of the ether
here. He still remembered the lecture from Da Vinci on the matter.
The mystery preserved in the deep sea meant a much higher density of ether along with it,
which his modern human body was terribly adapted to. Even with the protection of Medea’s
spell, that more than anything else weighed into him.
But that didn’t matter now, all he could do now was keep diving into the depths.
Soon, a vast floor loomed out of the darkness – solid, sandy, and pale, like the surface of the
moon. It felt strange – he was perhaps the first person to ever visit the seafloor here, and most
likely the only person who ever will. If Medea’s protections faltered even slightly here, then
that would be the end of him in the blink of an eye.
As he swam closer and the seafloor came into focus, his eyes widened mildly in surprise.
Instead of a barren wasteland, it was surprisingly teeming with life: starfish slowly but surely
making their paths toward new sources of food, crustaceans crawling about, rare tiny lights of
anglerfish, and more that he probably couldn’t see well.
It was beautiful in its own bizarre way. Alien and strange, yet colorful and shining. The lack
of light and extreme pressure of the depths molded the small beings, forcing them to adapt to
the inhospitable environment.
Despite everything, their smallness and frailty also made some part of him want to protect
them. A delicate system, perched on the edge of the abyss.
Then a larger fish hidden between rocks darted out to snatch up a smaller one. Life here knew
no peace, and just as it knew no ease, the corpse of another life drifting to the depths was all
the lifeline they had for the tiny denizens of this wasteland.
No matter how much you try, or work for so long, the smallest injustice can wipe it all out,
leave you with nothing… Don’t you, of all people, understand that!?
Maruki’s words echoed unbidden in his mind, much to his exhaustion. As much as he
opposed his former counselor, he felt that point was hard to argue, especially from where he

stood: scraping the depths of the ocean for what little scraps of strength after the end of the
world.
It would be easy to imagine his previous choice was a mistake like this, just as the starfish
desperately scavenged from what was left of a long decayed marlin.
But… they still fought, didn’t they? They still wanted to live. They had no hesitation; none of
the flitting creatures below him did. With the weight of the entire ocean on their backs, they
pushed forward regardless.
Despite everything, he smiled to himself. Even in this frigid, absolute darkness, life still
teemed and thrived. Through oppressive odds, living beings still carved out their paths as best
they could.
‘Master, is everything alright?’
Siegfried’s voice cut through his thoughts. ‘So far so good,’ he reported casually. ‘I just
reached the seafloor. It should be closer to swim over – I’m not seeing anything out of the
ordinary here.’
‘Very well,’ the dragonslayer acknowledged. ‘Do you have eyes on the treasure?’
‘Not yet, but it shouldn’t be too long,’ he replied. ‘I’ll let you know as soon as I have it.’
Sensing the acknowledgement from Siegfried, he cut off their mental contact. He activated
his Third Eye once again as he searched for the treasure. His already shrouded surroundings
darkened as he swam slowly in a circle, checking his surroundings for anything that stood
out.
Then a glimmer of blue light in the distance on the seafloor caught his attention. His eyes
widened and he began excitedly swimming towards it – and paused as a large, glowing
yellow light revealed itself right beside it underneath the seafloor. It was about the size of a
whale, easily dwarfing him. While it wasn’t hostile, he wasn’t sure how long that would last.
Ren crossed his arms as he considered his options. Before he could fully retrieve the treasure,
he needed to drop off at least some of it into the Velvet Room, which meant he couldn’t ask
the others to grab it immediately. Igor had asked him to keep the Room a secret and he had
no intention of breaking his promise.
He smirked as he decided. There wouldn’t be a better time to see how stealthy he could be
underwater.
Drifting down, he slowly and carefully made his way toward the treasure, keeping an eye on
the great yellow light. It was motionless as he approached, making sure to move his limbs as
little as possible and allowing his momentum to propel him forward instead. It was as still as
a statue, as though it was sleeping… or waiting.
Keeping low to the seafloor, he glided his way forward, weaving through rocky outcrops. He
gently pushed on a stone to propel him forward and gauged its reaction. Certain creatures, he

recalled, could detect the presence of others by vibrations either through water or the ground.
It was better to find out now than when he was almost right on top of it.
Yet still, the creature didn’t move in the slightest, nor did the yellow light change whatsoever.
Did it not notice him? While unnerving, for now, there was little other option than to continue
forward while keeping an eye on it.
Bit by bit, he made his way forward. He prowled and drifted through the darkness of the
depths, taking shallow breaths to minimize his disturbance through the water. The kelp-like
extensions fluttered and drifted alongside him, easily sliding through the water and helping
him move far faster than any regular human could.
Before long, he was at the chest – and almost right on top of the creature lurking beside it. Its
color hadn’t shifted still, nor had it moved in the slightest. He was thankfully at its side,
meaning it needed to turn if it became hostile. It would buy him a precious few seconds to
escape if worse came to worse.
Floating down to the treasure chest, the Phantom Thief mentally adjusted his Third Eye.
Right now, he simply needed the chest to stop glowing so he could see what he was doing.
He blinked – and suddenly it was no longer blinding, but the creature was still shining just as
brightly as before.
Ren smiled in satisfaction. Exactly what he needed.
He made his way closer to the chest until he could pick out its details. Medea’s enchantments
didn’t grant him the best vision in absolute darkness of the murky depths, but it sufficed. It
was a box made of a green-like metal, etched with all sorts of reliefs that he couldn’t make
out with his limited vision, all sealed by an elaborate, complex-looking lock in front.
Reaching into his jacket, he took out his perma-pick set and got to work, first feeling out the
pins through his lockpick. It was trickier than usual: the water around him combined with the
frigid temperature made feeling out the pins and shear lines considerably more difficult.
Being afloat also meant he couldn’t turn the torsion wrench as well either.
Then there was the lock itself. While its mechanisms were thankfully similar to regular locks,
it was still more complex than a normal padlock, and the hindered visibility certainly didn’t
help in that regard either.
However, none of those factors deterred Ren. Instead, he found himself enjoying the new
puzzle laid before him. This was the most fun bit of lockpicking he had done in a long while.
And the creature either slumbering or simply unaware of his presence nearby only added
more spice to the challenge.
Slowly but surely he worked, pushing the pins to their respective shear lines and twisting the
torque wrench to lock them in place. Its unorthodox shaping and construction made it
difficult, but he adjusted easily enough. It was simply making sure none of his progress was
undone as he continued.

Every so often he glanced over at the creature burrowed beside him, watching for any signs
of movement. At times, he wasn’t sure if the yellow light representing the creature shifted or
if it was just a trick of the eye. Yet in the end, he continued working.
Finally, the lock clicked, turned, and opened. Immediately the lid was flung back as air
bubbles burst out, burbling loudly as they vanished into the darkness above. The Phantom
Thief immediately whirled to check if the creature reacted, ready to bolt if necessary.
A moment passed. Then another. He could feel a shiver down his spine as he waited for the
creature’s reaction.
Then the creature began shifting, alarming Ren enough that he started swimming backwards,
trying to gain distance from it. However, it seemed to be burrowing itself deeper instead of
surfacing. The unknown beast soon fell still again, and the silence of the depths pervaded
once more.
Ren blinked in surprise, then breathed a small sigh of relief. It seemed like things worked out
for him, but he wasn’t about to linger for much longer. Carefully swimming back down, he
looked over the contents of the chest – and his eyes widened at what he saw.
Gold.
The chest was practically overflowing with gold coins. It wasn’t regular gold either – it
shimmered and almost seemed to glow faintly despite the darkness of the seafloor. He
delicately picked one up and looked it over. Etched on it were symbols and iconography he
couldn’t recognize for the life of him. Maybe Drake would know.
In the meantime, he accomplished his goal. Now he just needed to deposit the gold – and
right on cue, there was a faint glow next to the treasure chest. Looking over, he saw a familiar
looking drop box glimmering with the ever-present blue of the Velvet Room.
Reaching up to the treasure chest, he began scooping handfuls of gold coins and dropped
them in. He idly wondered how much would be enough to satisfy its conditions. If he took
too much, Drake would be suspicious and the resulting confrontation would be troublesome.
After about the tenth handful, the door to the drop box slid out of his grasp almost
inadvertently. It closed, then faded from view into nothing. The Phantom Thief couldn’t help
but blink again in mild surprise. He expected to deposit a lot more but if that was all Igor and
Lavenza needed, he wasn’t about to complain.
Looking over the treasure, he gently smoothed over the considerable remainder of the gold
coins to make them seem as undisturbed as possible. Once he was satisfied with it, he
reached up and closed the lid, hearing the lock slide back into place with a click. Now that he
opened it once, it would most likely be easier to open again once it was brought up to the
surface.
Taking out the ball of yarn Morgana had given him, he wrapped a string around the chest and
tied it off, then he began swimming back toward Tarrasque, following the tugging feeling

Medea had enchanted on him. As he did, he unspooled the yarn, the vivid red string only
barely visible in the darkness.
‘Senpai?’ Mash called out worriedly. ‘You’re taking a while – is everything okay?’
‘Hey Mash,’ he replied cheerfully. ‘I’m fine. Sorry for the quiet – I was focused on the
treasure and it took me a while. But I found it and I’m on the way back now.’
‘Oh, that’s good,’ the Shielder breathed. He could feel her sheer relief through their mental
connection. ‘We were about to set off in search for you. You had been quiet for so long, after
all.’
‘Sorry about that,’ Ren apologized with a rueful laugh. ‘At least we have the treasure now.
Fair warning though, there’s something nesting in the ground right beside it. About the size of
a whale. Didn’t seem all too hostile when I was over there but with Tarrasque, I’ve no clue
how it’ll react.’
There was a moment of silence, then Mash replied, ‘Martha said Tarrasque should be able to
handle it. Very well done, senpai!’
He grinned. ‘All in a day’s work for a Phantom Thief,’ he casually acknowledged.
Before long, the figure of the dragon loomed out of the darkness as he approached, followed
by the figures of his very concerned Servants and Mash. They followed the thread toward the
treasure chest, keeping an eye out for any predators that sought to ambush them. Before long,
they were right over it.
‘Where is the creature?’ Siegfried asked, squinting into the seafloor below to catch sight of it.
Ren looked around with this Third Eye, then pointed. ‘Right over there,’ he answered.
Then suddenly, it shifted and began scurrying away, causing the seafloor above to collapse –
and the chest began sinking into the ground with it. ‘Crap. Grab it!’ he ordered.
Tarrasque swooped in and, with surprising dexterity for its size, scooped up the treasure chest
in a great claw. Dirt and rubble cascaded down as the dragon secured its hold. ‘Tarrasque has
the treasure, Master,’ Martha announced with a smile.
The Phantom Thief grinned. ‘Great job, everyone,’ he congratulated. ‘Especially you,
Tarrasque. Remind me to treat you sometime for your work.’ The dragon let out a pleased
huff in response. ‘Now, let’s head back up – I’m calling this a successful expedition.’
He took his seat behind Mash again, wrapping his arms securely around her waist. The
Shielder gulped before placing a hand over his to make sure he was in place - and no other
reason.
Martha spared a glance over at the two, smiled then transmitted her thoughts to Tarrasque.
‘Let’s go,’ she commanded.

The Tarrasque let out a growl of affirmation before turning with surprising alacrity and began
swimming upward. They held out tightly to its shell as they rapidly ascended from the
depths, leaving the seafloor behind.
Ren couldn’t help but take one last look back. The creatures there would continue their life as
they always had. Their visit was ultimately irrelevant. They would continue to strive,
struggle, carve out their place, and survive as best they could.
How resilient.
‘Something amusing, Master?’ Siegfried asked curiously.
The Phantom Thief didn’t even notice he was smiling again. ‘No, nothing,’ he brushed off.
‘Just happy to be here.’
The dragonslayer nodded with a smile of his own. ‘As are we,’ he replied before facing
forward again.
With each stroke of Tarrasque’s mighty limbs, they kept climbing and climbing. The depths
around them slowly brightened, darkness yielding back to blue as the sea above them started
almost glowing. Though they didn’t encounter any more aquatic life, they kept watch
regardless for anything hostile.
Azure gave way to cerulean, then to aquamarine as they neared the surface. The glow above
steadily became brighter and brighter, then started breaking as the waves became visible. As
they ascended, a school of fish flowed around them like a silver river, breaking in either
direction as they swam past.
Ren and Mash couldn’t help but stare in wonder as they passed by. ‘I wonder where they’re
going,’ the former mused.
‘Maybe migrating to a new feeding ground?’ the Shielder suggested as they watched the fish
vanish into blue beyond. ‘Schools like these often have to for reproduction purposes. It’s a
dangerous journey with so many predators out at sea, so they congregate in such numbers as
a method of defense.’
‘Strength in numbers, huh?’ the Phantom Thief chuckled. ‘That sounds rather familiar.’
Moments later, they finally surfaced some distance from the Golden Hind with a great splash,
seafoam splashing everywhere. Ren blinked as his eyes adjusted to pure sunlight again, then
stretched. The warmth of the surface was almost blazing compared to the coolness of the sea
or the cold of the depths. He took a deep breath, relishing the fresh air.
He had enjoyed his time diving into the sea, but the surface and land was where he belonged.
Well, not that enough treasure couldn’t persuade him back down into the depths. He couldn’t
even pretend to have that much restraint.
Tarrasque began swimming back toward the ship with a more casual pace, almost drifting
like a gigantic piece of flotsam. Ren glanced up to see the others gathering on the side of the

ship and raised a hand.
“Ahoy there!” he called out. “We miss much?”
“A bunch of mermaids and sirens swam right by crooning their hearts out!” Drake yelled
back with a broad grin. “Shame you weren’t here – they were probably your type!”
The Phantom Thief laughed. “A shame indeed!” he agreed. “But I do have priorities here!”
“You got the treasure?!” Morgana cried, almost bouncing on the banister.
“You’ll see!” he shouted back. His grin widened when Morgana groaned in frustration in
response as Drake and the crew laughed heartily.
Once they reached the Golden Hind, Drake’s crew tossed sets of ropes over the side. As the
others ascended, Ren grabbed a set of ropes, dived off Tarrasque, and tied them to the chest.
When he was done, he resurfaced and waved.
At the Phantom Thief’s signal, the sailors grabbed their ropes and began hauling up the
treasure chest up the side of the ship. “Heave! Ho! Heave! Ho!” they chanted, pulling in
rhythm. Siegfried, Martha, Joan, Ritsuka, and Mash joined in while Morgana kept watch over
the side of the ship, making sure nothing went wrong.
Ren meanwhile stayed perched on the chest, a hand on the rope to support himself. As he
approached the banister, he hopped up and mantled over before seizing a rope and helped pull
the remaining distance. Once the chest was high enough, Siegfried and Martha grabbed it and
hoisted it onto the deck, placing it down with a solid thunk.
Drake stepped forward, looking over the chest with an appraising eye. The greenish metal
gleamed with surprising luster under the afternoon sun, with almost no tarnish or blemish
despite its time in the depths. Engravings were carefully cast and carved on the sides and lid,
displaying symbols and scenes of the container’s owner.
Ritsuka looked it over in curiosity. “... the art looks a bit like what I’ve seen on Greek
pottery,” she quietly commented. “But… different somehow? Not sure how besides the fact
it’s metal, not paint on clay.”
“Ya got a good eye, Red,” the captain praised with a grin. “But you’re slightly off the mark
there. The treasure we got here ain’t Greek, but pretty damn close. Hell, I’ll bet you anything
the box itself here is worth a fortune - it’s not rusted bronze or brass, that’s for sure.” She
gave it a small kick for emphasis.
With that, she whirled around as her eyes glittered with excitement and greed. “Oi, Joker,”
Drake barked out. “Get this hunk of junk open!”
The Phantom Thief smirked as he slipped out his perma-pick for the second time today.
“Your wish is my command,” he acknowledged with a graceful bow.
Ren grinned, knelt by the lock, and started his work. As he expected, it was far easier to
lockpick the chest above water and with proper lighting despite its complexity. The pins and

shear lines felt completely obvious in comparison with his now unhindered senses, allowing
him to easily lock them in place.
In a fraction of the time, the lock once again clicked open. He flung back the lid - and jumped
back as water splashed out of the chest and onto the deck. Sitting within were the
innumerable gold coins bathed in seawater, gleaming fiercely in the daylight like a thousand
suns.
Drake looked over approvingly with a fierce grin. “Looks like your headings were right on
the mark after all, Joker!” she cried, smacking him hard on the back. “We have a helluva haul
here! They need to be appraised, but I bet my pistols they’re purer than even the finest
goldsmiths can make! Just a few handfuls of these would set anyone for life!”
The sailors immediately broke out cheering and laughing. “We’re gonna be rich!” one of
them hollered. “All hail the captain, and all hail Joker!”
“Right, this is our biggest haul in a while!” Drake roared out. “We’re having a party tonight!
Siegfried, haul up the kegs from the hold! Jackson! Smith! Drain the water from the chest
and get this all stowed away in my cabin! The rest of you lot, unfurl the sails! We got a nice
wind blowing by, and I ain’t gonna miss it for the life of me!”
The sailors shouted back in assent and immediately went back to work. The two that Drake
called out grabbed the chest and started dragging it to the side of the ship to drain the
seawater. Meanwhile, the captain followed to make sure none of the coins got loose – either
by accident or sticky fingers.
She walked by Ren, who was stretching in the open air. “You know, looking at that chest,”
Drake remarked casually. “It’s pretty damn well constructed - enough to be watertight, I’ll
wager. The inside would’ve been nice and dry until the world’s end. What’d you think?”
The Phantom Thief looked over at her with a smirk. “Maybe it’s just a faulty chest,” he
suggested. “They can’t all be masterpieces of craftsmanship. And it’s been down there for a
while too – could’ve sprung a leak.”
“Ya think so, hm?” the captain mused, watching her men slowly drain the water from the
chest. “Well then, so long as the gold is more or less untouched, I suppose I’ll leave it at that.
Just remember, a good treasure is supposed to be shared – and the captain decides who gets
what.”
As her eyes bored into Ren, his smirk widened. “True, but when it comes to business
ventures, unexpected expenditures do happen,” he retorted. “Especially when you hire
freelancers. Finder’s fees, for example.”
They stared one another down, then Drake let out a chuckle. “Fair enough, Joker,” she
relented. “You and yours have earned your fair share here. Just remember your dues – not just
here but anywhere else, or you’re gonna find yourself in a debtor’s prison before long.”
“Already been to jail once, technically,” the Phantom Thief retorted. “But I’ll keep that in
mind.”

The captain let out a guffaw at his response before sauntering off to take a closer look at the
treasure as Ritsuka walked up with a concerned expression. “Everything alright between you
and the captain?” she asked.
“Just a friendly chat between some rogues,” he easily answered, turning toward her. “Come
on, we better help with the setup. Tonight’s party is gonna be loud.”
“I swear, all these guys ever do is party,” Ritsuka grumbled, nevertheless following her senior
Master.
The raucous laughs and cheers of the sailors rang across the sea. It had been truly a fruitful
day for all of them.
---------“Still got eyes on them?”
“Aye, captain,” the woman replied from the crow’s nest. “They’re a couple leagues away, but
no one’s keeping watch. Guess they’re celebratin’ something.”
“Oho? And is our ever so lovely goddess on board?”
“Right on the shoulders of the big, horned one,” she answered. “She sticks out like a sore
thumb among the others.”
“Seems like things are going well, captain,” a man commented as he walked up before
leaning on a nearby mast. “Orders?”
A hook tapped on the railing in contemplation, then lifted off. “What else? Load the guns and
full speed ahead!” he cried out. “We’re gonna catch ‘em with their pants down!”
“Aye aye, captain!” the sailors chorused.
The captain grinned in anticipation as the Jolly Roger was tied to the mast in preparation. He
might not be the terror of the seas anymore, but they would still learn to fear his name.
